findings.consequent: number of correctly recalled stated words (overall)
findings.mechanism: more resource demanding item identification becomes when the RT is too long, leaving less time for transfer to long-term storage
findings.quote: Significantly fewer stated words were recalled in the Long RT than in the Short RT condition... F (1, 30) = 7.67, p=.01, η2 = .20.

findings.consequent: number of correctly recalled words (first two parts of list)
findings.mechanism: more resource demanding item identification becomes when the RT is too long, impairing encoding and early consolidation
findings.quote: recall of the first two parts of the list only was affected by RT. This was reflected in an interaction between condition and parts in the linear trend F (1, 30) = 10.16; p = .003, η2= .25.

findings.consequent: number of correctly recalled words (last part of list)
findings.mechanism: the RT effect was pronounced at the beginning of the word list but was absent in the last part of the list, suggesting distraction effects of noise in previous study
findings.quote: the RT effect was pronounced at the beginning of the word list but was absent in the last part of the list.

findings.consequent: frequency of extra list errors (words not part of list)
findings.mechanism: inhibitory control was less efficient in bad listening conditions
findings.quote: Extra list errors were significantly less frequent in the short than in the long RT condition (means: 2.2 and 3.1, z= 2.22, p = .03).

findings.mechanism: recognition of sentences was less sensitive to the long RT
findings.quote: A two-way ANOVA (condition x presentation order) showed no significant difference between the conditions regarding the number of correct responses of Hagerman’s sentences.

findings.consequent: response time to identify irrelevant sentences
findings.mechanism: longer processing time to sort out irrelevant sentences, as this task is more demanding
findings.quote: when sentences were heard in the short RT condition the participants were faster to identify the sentences that not had been presented... F (1, 31) = 4.62, p = .04, η2 = .13).

findings.antecedent: reading span score (working memory capacity) * long reverberation time (mean RT 1.17 s)
findings.mechanism: reading span performance was unrelated to performance in both the word list and sentence task as well as to the effect of RT
findings.quote: Contrary to expectations, reading span performance was unrelated to performance in both the word list and sentence task as well as to the effect of RT in these tests.

findings.mechanism: poor listening conditions impair memory and learning, even if speech is intelligible, by increasing cognitive load
findings.quote: The participants’ memory performance was worse when the lecture was heard in the noise condition... F(1, 26) = 6.71, MSE = 1.23, p < .05, η2 = .20

findings.mechanism: long reverberation time disrupts memory for lectures, even when speech is equally intelligible, by increasing cognitive load
findings.quote: The participants’ memory performance was worse when the lecture was heard with a long reverberation time... F(1, 17) = 16.60, MSE = 2.12, p < .001, η2 = .49

findings.mechanism: participants rated their hearing of the lecture equally well in both conditions
findings.quote: These two means did not differ significantly, as shown by a paired t-test, t(18) < 1.

findings.consequent: proportion correct serial recall of meaningful words
findings.mechanism: the effect of degraded stimuli on memory only appears when lexical-identity of words forms the basis of retrieval, not serial order processing
findings.quote: A 3(Reverberation time) × 8(serial position) analysis of variance revealed no effect of Reverberation time, F(2, 58) = 1.46, MSE = 5.03, p = 0.24

findings.consequent: mean recall for primacy part of word list
findings.mechanism: word activation overload due to degraded stimuli leads to lower correct recall
findings.quote: Follow-up tests showed that the RevT condition differed from control in the primacy part of the list (t = 3.91, p < .01).

findings.antecedent: degraded listening conditions (long RevT or low S/N)
findings.mechanism: The main effect of listening condition was not significant
findings.quote: The main effect of listening condition was not significant, F(2, 46) = 2.62, MSE = 0.16, p = .084

findings.antecedent: degraded listening conditions (long RevT or low S/N) * serial position (quadratic trend)
findings.mechanism: degraded stimuli activate more phonological neighbors, leading to word activation overload, especially in the primacy part
findings.quote: there was a significant interaction between condition and position in the quadratic trend, F(1, 23) = 4.91, MSE = 0.09 p < .05, η2 = 0.18.

findings.antecedent: high delayed intrusions in OSPAN (working memory capacity) * low S/N ratio
findings.mechanism: people who fail to suppress or delete stored information from earlier tasks are more vulnerable to noise
findings.quote: delayed intrusions were significantly related to the effect of noise on the primacy score (b = -0.51, t = 3.69, p < .001).

findings.antecedent: high inventions in OSPAN (working memory capacity) * low S/N ratio
findings.mechanism: degradation of stimuli activates more phonological candidates, and people with many OSPAN inventions have problems suppressing them
findings.quote: people who made many invention errors in OSPAN performed significantly more false recall in low S/N (Experimant1b)

findings.mechanism: degraded speech signals impair categorical-lexical based free recall
findings.quote: fewer words were recalled when the lists was presented with the longer RevT (means: 3.06 and 2.78, respectively; F(1, 23) = 13.25, MSE = 0.44, p <.001, η2 = 0.37).

findings.antecedent: word lists with many phonological neighbors * serial position (quadratic trend)
findings.mechanism: high neighborhood density activates more competing candidates, requiring more inhibition which can impair recall
findings.quote: the trend over Serial Positions differed between lists containing words with few or many Phonological Neighbors, F(1, 23) = 6.47, MSE = 0.18, p < .05, η2 = .22).

findings.antecedent: word lists with many phonological neighbors (mid part of list)
findings.mechanism: temporal distinctiveness theory: middle words are least distinctive and more vulnerable to lexical interference
findings.quote: Follow-up tests showed that the significant effect of neighbors was only obtained in the mid part of the list t(23) = 2.47, p < 0.05.

findings.antecedent: high inventions in OSPAN (working memory capacity) * phonological neighbor word lists
findings.consequent: effect of phonological neighbor word lists
findings.mechanism: people who make invention errors in OSPAN cannot inhibit activated neighbors properly, leading to recall of wrong words
findings.quote: The effect of phonological neighbours was significantly related to the number of inventions in OSPAN, b = -.29, t(21) = 2.12, p < .05.

findings.antecedent: high number of correctly recalled words in OSPAN (working memory capacity) * long reverberation time
findings.mechanism: higher working memory capacity provides more resources for processing in degraded conditions
findings.quote: The effect of long RevT on the primacy part of the list was significantly related to the number of correctly recalled words in the operation span task, b = .58, t(21) = 2.99, p < .01.

findings.antecedent: high number of correctly recalled words in OSPAN (working memory capacity) * long reverberation time
findings.mechanism: higher working memory capacity provides more resources for processing in degraded conditions
findings.quote: This relation was also significant for the mid part of the lists task, b = .29, t(21) = 2.49, p < .05.

findings.antecedent: high delayed intrusions in OSPAN (working memory capacity) * long reverberation time
findings.mechanism: people who fail to suppress or delete stored information from earlier tasks are more vulnerable to noise
findings.quote: For the recency part the effect was significantly related to delayed intrusions, b = -.55, t(21) = 2.90, p < .01.

limitations: Paper I: Large sampling errors made correlations unreliable, requiring replications.
Paper I: Sound context difference between presentation and recall in noise condition might have contributed to the effect.
Paper I: Sentence recognition task might have been too easy, leading to no significant effect on error rate.
Paper II: Wide confidence intervals of correlations in a group of 32 persons require further studies for definite conclusions.
Paper II: Need to test effects on more realistic learning tasks (longer spoken texts) for better acoustical norms.
Paper III: Previous studies (e.g., Rabbitt) had methodological issues like group testing and lack of control for individual differences in memory capacity or speech perception abilities.
Paper IV: All results of memory performance could be an effect of incorrect word identification.
Paper IV: Repeating stimuli during experiments might lead to better recall performance than in real-world scenarios, potentially underestimating the true effects of degraded conditions.
